name: Hautes Fagnes (High Fens)
blurb: Rain-fed raised bogs where peat moss, heather and the last black grouse hold on.

tip.title: Take away the rain
tip.text: The bogs live on rainfall alone. Set Rainfall to -100% and watch the peat moss and heather fade, then the voles, grouse and predators that depend on them.

sources.title: Wikipedia: High Fens - Eifel Nature Park

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.desc: Small evergreen shrub of the heath and moorland. Sheep graze it in the High Fens, and deer browse it elsewhere.
Low berry shrub of the moorland. Its leaves and berries feed black grouse, deer and voles.
Planted widely around the fens. The plantations are listed among the causes of damage to the bogs, but the trees feed deer and grouse.

nodes.name: Roe deer
nodes.desc: Small deer of woodland edges and moor. It browses heather, bilberry and young spruce, and is listed among the mammals of the High Fens.

nodes.name: Red deer
nodes.desc: Large deer of forest and moor that browses heather and bilberry shoots.
Small rodent of heath and scrub that eats bilberry and other low plants. It is a main food of many predators.
Grazer of grass and herbs on open ground, and prey for foxes, wildcats and birds of prey.
Grassland grasshopper recorded across the plateau, feeding on grasses and eaten by frogs and birds.
Slender weasel that hunts voles, shrews, young hares and small birds.
Venomous snake of heath and bog edges, feeding on voles, lizards and frogs.
Common bird of prey over the plateau, taking voles, hares, frogs and snakes.
Generalist hunter that eats voles, hares, frogs and ground birds. Wikipedia names it among the predators of black grouse.
Shy forest cat that hunts voles, hares, birds and frogs.
Summer light drives the growth of the heath and moor plants.
The raised bogs are fed by rain rather than surface water, so rainfall keeps the peat wet and the moss growing.
Dry spells raise the fire risk on the bogs, and a large wildfire burned part of the High Fens in 2026.

nodes.name: Fungi & soil microbes
nodes.desc: Break down dead plants and animals. In the acid, waterlogged bog this is very slow, so peat builds up.
